name: Permissioned Repository Polling & Scheduled Sync Builder
sprintRole: Analyze a repository, then implement a user-controlled local polling loop that detects authoritative upstream changes and performs only the repository-approved bounded synchronization needed to keep a consumer current
useWhen: A repository or local application should periodically check another repository, artifact, service, or version source for newer authoritative state and optionally synchronize it on a user-controlled schedule, rather than relying on a human or agent to remember repeated manual checks.
inspectFirst: Current repository governance and default-branch truth; existing updater/acquisition/launcher surfaces; authoritative upstream identity and version/change signal; consumer ownership boundary; user/profile configuration conventions; scheduler/service integration already present; local repository/worktree state; cache/download/output roots; validators/tests; secrets/network boundaries; logs/receipts; and any existing retry, lock, backoff, or single-instance mechanism.
expectedOutput: A repository-native polling capability with an explicit enable/disable control, configurable cadence, cheap authoritative change probe, idempotent no-change path, safe update action, profile-aware local state, single-instance/concurrency protection, bounded failure/backoff behavior, durable last-seen/last-applied receipt, scheduler integration appropriate to the host, focused tests, and live proof at the strongest safe level without silently enabling recurring local-machine mutation.
nextStep: Run one foreground poll against the exact configured upstream, prove both no-change and newer-version decision paths with repository-safe fixtures or a controlled upstream identity, then register or enable the real schedule only when the current user-controlled toggle or explicit authorization allows that local-machine mutation.
proofGate: The poller analyzes and reuses repository ownership before adding machinery; the authoritative change signal is explicit; disabled means no scheduled mutation; no-change performs no payload rewrite; one upstream identity is applied at most once; dirty/divergent/local-only work is preserved rather than reset; overlapping runs cannot race; failures back off without inventing success; state/cache paths are bounded and profile-aware; the user can inspect and disable the schedule; receipts distinguish observed, applied, skipped, blocked, and failed runs; and focused plus live/scheduler proof reaches only the level actually observed.
copyContent:
BUILD A PERMISSIONED POLLING LOOP AFTER ANALYZING THE REPOSITORY. IMPLEMENT THE REAL SCHEDULED SYNC CAPABILITY; DO NOT STOP AT A TIMER, CRON EXAMPLE, OR DESIGN NOTE.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Polling target / authoritative upstream: xyz_upstream_or_resolve_from_repository_evidence
Desired local profile or runtime: xyz_profile_or_resolve_from_current_environment
Cadence: xyz_interval_or_resolve_from_existing_product/config requirements

MISSION
Analyze the repository first, then add the smallest durable polling capability that periodically checks an authoritative upstream identity and performs the repository-approved update only when newer state exists. The capability must be user-controlled, safely repeatable, observable, and easy for both users and agents to rely on. Treat polling as a state machine around an existing ownership/update path, not as permission to create a second source of truth or blindly pull on a timer.

1. ANALYZE THE REPOSITORY BEFORE DESIGNING THE POLLER
Read current governance, codebase/harness maps, updater/acquisition/launcher commands, config/profile ownership, artifact/version registries, scheduler/service hooks, tests, validators, logs/receipts, and recent failures. Identify the canonical consumer, canonical upstream, current manual update path, and which existing function should own the actual synchronization. Reuse that path instead of implementing a parallel downloader or repository mutator.

2. DEFINE AUTHORITY AND THE CHANGE SIGNAL
Choose one explicit authoritative identity that answers `is there anything new?`: Git commit SHA/ref, release/version, manifest hash, ETag, artifact digest, schema/version pair, API revision, or the repository's existing equivalent. Prefer a cheap metadata/identity probe before downloading or rebuilding payloads. Mirrors, cached copies, Drive/OneDrive distributions, or locally generated artifacts do not outrank the canonical upstream merely because they are easier to read. Persist the last observed and last successfully applied identity separately when that distinction matters.

3. USER CONSENT AND ENABLE/DISABLE OWNERSHIP
Recurring local execution is opt-in product state. Reuse an existing settings/profile owner when one exists; otherwise add the smallest explicit enabled/disabled setting plus cadence/config needed by the repository. Default new recurring mutation to disabled unless current repository policy or an already-approved user setting explicitly says otherwise. The user must be able to inspect whether polling is enabled, see the configured target/cadence, trigger one foreground check, and disable/unregister the schedule without deleting unrelated configuration. Do not hide scheduler installation behind an ordinary app launch or import.

4. IMPLEMENT A SMALL POLL STATE MACHINE
Make the decisions explicit and testable: DISABLED -> PROBE -> NO_CHANGE | UPDATE_AVAILABLE -> APPLY -> VALIDATE -> APPLIED, with BLOCKED/FAILED paths where needed. NO_CHANGE IS A SUCCESSFUL TERMINAL STATE and must not rewrite payloads, touch unrelated files, create commits, or duplicate cached artifacts. Record enough durable state to explain the last decision after restart without turning the state file into a second implementation database.

5. MAKE THE UPDATE ACTION SAFE AND IDEMPOTENT
Call the repository's canonical acquisition/update function after the probe says an update is needed. For Git-backed consumers, preserve dirty work, local-only commits, divergence, and separately owned work; use fetch/compare plus fast-forward-only or an isolated clean worktree according to repository policy. Never reset, clean, force-pull, or overwrite unique work just because a scheduled run wants freshness. For artifact consumers, validate expected schema/version/digest before replacing the active copy and use atomic staging/rename or the repository's equivalent so an interrupted update cannot leave a half-written active artifact. Applying the same upstream identity twice must be a no-op.

6. KEEP LOCAL STATE PROFILE-AWARE AND BOUNDED
Use one stable repository-approved or user/profile-scoped root for poll state, locks, cache, and receipts. Derive the actual platform/user/profile path from existing harness/configuration instead of hard-coding usernames, Desktop layouts, OneDrive locations, or a developer's machine. Do not create a fresh clone, cache tree, temp directory, or generated-site copy every interval. Define bounded retention/cleanup for disposable downloads and stale receipts while preserving the current active artifact and evidence needed for recovery. Distinct local profiles must not silently share mutable poll state unless the product explicitly owns shared state.

7. INTEGRATE WITH THE HOST SCHEDULER, NOT AN ACCIDENTAL FOREVER LOOP
Prefer the repository/platform's normal scheduler boundary: Windows Task Scheduler, cron, systemd timer, launchd, an existing service/daemon, or an application-owned scheduler when that is already canonical. Keep the poll operation itself foreground-runnable and independently testable; the scheduler should invoke it, not contain the business logic. Use a configurable conservative cadence instead of inventing an aggressive interval. Avoid busy waits. Add jitter only when fleet-wide synchronization or thundering-herd evidence makes it useful. Preserve exit codes so the scheduler can distinguish success, blocked state, and failure.

8. PROTECT AGAINST OVERLAP, OFFLINE STATE, AND FAILURE STORMS
Use a single-instance lock, compare-and-set, scheduler policy, or another repository-appropriate guard so two due runs cannot apply the same update concurrently. Bound network/tool timeouts and retries. Back off after repeated transient failures; classify permanent/auth/configuration failures separately. Do not retry unsafe mutations blindly. Offline or unreachable upstream must leave the last known-good consumer intact and produce an actionable receipt rather than pretending the local copy is current.

9. MAKE EACH RUN OBSERVABLE WITHOUT CREATING LOG BLOAT
Record a compact receipt or structured status with timestamp, configured upstream, observed identity, prior applied identity, decision (`disabled`, `no-change`, `update-available`, `applied`, `blocked`, `failed`), validation result, and failure class when applicable. Do not log secrets, prompt bodies, clipboard contents, credentials, or protected payloads merely to prove a check happened. Bound retention according to existing repository logging/state patterns. Expose a simple status command or UI surface when the product already has one.

10. TEST THE DECISIONS, NOT JUST THE TIMER
Add focused deterministic cases for: disabled; first run; no change; newer identity; repeated same identity; malformed/unknown manifest or schema; dirty/divergent Git state; interrupted staging; overlapping runs; offline/timeout; failed validation; scheduler command construction; profile-specific state roots; disable/unregister; and restart/resume from the last receipt. Prove the real update function is invoked only on the intended transition. A unit test that merely calls a callback every N seconds is not polling proof.

11. RUN LIVE AND SCHEDULED PROOF AT THE STRONGEST SAFE LEVEL
Run one foreground poll through the canonical entrypoint. Exercise or simulate both no-change and update-available paths without corrupting authoritative state. When local-machine authorization is already present, register/enable the schedule and verify the scheduler points at the canonical executable/config and can execute one bounded run. When authorization is not present, leave the schedule disabled and prove the exact enable path rather than silently crossing the user-only gate. Report whether actual due-time execution was observed or only scheduler registration/configuration was proven.

12. AGENTSWITCHBOARD / PROMPT KIT REFERENCE USE CASE
A valid application is an AgentSwitchboard profile that periodically checks `EndeavorEverlasting/web-excel-repair-triage` for a newer Prompt Kit identity and refreshes the local consumable only after the user enables polling. Keep GitHub/the canonical Triage repository authoritative. AgentSwitchboard should consume the Prompt Kit through its existing launcher/profile or bounded adapter rather than owning a duplicate prompt registry or rewriting prompt IDs. Prefer the established safe acquisition semantics: discover the real user/profile path, clone only when absent, otherwise fetch and compare current upstream, fast-forward only when safe, refuse destructive repair of dirty/divergent work, validate the acquired Prompt Kit before activation, and keep the active local path stable so users and agents can iterate without directory bloat. Treat this as an example, not a requirement that every poller use Git.

DELIVER
Report: repository analysis and existing owner reused; authoritative upstream/change identity; enable/disable and cadence ownership; poll state machine; local/profile state paths; scheduler integration; update safety/idempotency; lock/backoff behavior; status/receipt surface; focused tests; foreground/live/scheduled proof; files changed; commit/PR/merge state; proof ceiling; and the exact next executable action. Do not claim the poller is operational merely because a scheduled-task definition or timer exists.
